claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is a homogeneous, single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy in the specified initial state.
Elemental size mismatch produces intrinsic lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal-expansion mismatch among the constituent elements creates local residual stresses during heating or cooling.
Local residual stresses promote thermally activated short-range ordering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Aging at 600–800 °C permits or facilitates the development of short-range order.
Thermal cycling enhances local residual-stress fields.
Short-range order alters the alloy's elastic response.
Residual stresses and the resulting short-range order govern the alloy's creep behavior.
Residual stresses and the resulting short-range order govern the alloy's hardening behavior.
Residual stresses and the resulting short-range order govern the alloy's thermoelastic behavior.
Samples conditioned by thermal cycling and aging will have greater creep resistance at 1250 °C than rapidly quenched baseline samples.
Conditioned samples will have higher post-cold-rolling microhardness than rapidly quenched baseline samples.
Conditioned samples will exhibit a distinct temperature dependence of elastic moduli over 293–1100 K relative to rapidly quenched baseline samples.
Rapid quenching after homogenization suppresses residual-stress development.
Rapid quenching after homogenization suppresses short-range ordering.
The proposed mechanism is significant within the 600–800 °C aging window.
The proposed mechanism becomes particularly influential near 1250 °C during tensile creep.
The effects of the proposed mechanism are less pronounced outside the specified aging and creep temperature ranges.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that cooling creates thermal-expansion-mismatch residual stresses, whereas the baseline assumes that rapid cooling by quenching minimizes those stresses. The hypothesis does not explain why rapid quenching would suppress rather than intensify cooling-induced stress.
